newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmers keep up blockade after talks fail.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmers keep up blockade after talks fail.

text.p: Defiant Greek farmers looked set to continue a week-long blockade of road and rail links on Thursday using thousands of tractors after talks with the government failed to reach agreement.

"The talks were fruitless. The agriculture minister repeated the government's known positions which don't satisfy us. We will meet to decide how to continue our action," a farmers' representative told reporters late on Wednesday.

Agriculture Minister Stephanos Tzoumakas held lengthy talks with the farmers at which he repeated that the state could not afford to satisfy their demands for better prices, cheaper fuel and rescheduling $1.3 billion in debts.

"Satisfying such demands would cost about $4 billion. This is impossible under the current circumstances and would upset the entire convergence programme with the European Union," an agriculture ministry official said.
Farmers had expected Prime Minister Costas Simitis, who chaired Wednesday's cabinet meeting, to make new proposals but he was in no mood for compromise.
Simitis, who won September elections, is facing the toughest challenge so far to his economic plans, which give priority to meeting European Union convergence targets.

Taking a tough line after the cabinet meeting, Tzoumakas told farmers: "The positions of the government stand. We have nothing new to propose (to the farmers). Those who have erected blockades should...remove them and free the roads."
An army of more than 10,000 colourful tractors has fanned out across Greece, seizing toll booths and blockading national road and rail links at more than 40 points.
Sprawling tent cities line major roads, with tables, chairs, food and drink. Groups of farmers sit around bonfires for warmth.
Border roads to Bulgaria and Turkey have been blocked, stopping all traffic. The entrance to Salonika international airport, Greece's second city and main northern port, is cut.
The blockade began last Thursday and has left hundreds of international and domestic lorries stranded. Drivers have been complaining about lack of food, water and sanitation.
Food merchants said stocks remain high, and prices largely under control, but have warned customers that if the protests continue next week there will be real problems.
"Of course the prices will go up. Where are we going to get meat from? They will have to go up," butcher Paulos Zachos told Reuters at the central Athens meat market.
Simitis stripped away many tax exemptions last week when he submitted his 1997 austerity budget and is facing opposition from other groups as well.

Pensioners, housewives, teachers, tax and port officials, and the civil servants union have all called strikes. Dockers have been on strike for a week over pension rights, and cargo has gone unloaded.
